## Procedure

> **[Partial]** Needs more work: the verifier could confirm only part of this procedure (the steps marked [Partial], or whether the list is complete). Steps or precautions may be wrong or missing; read the source thread before relying on it. Later runs fill it in as more sources are found.

1. [Partial] Identify the specific area on the fender requiring modification.
2. Heat the inside corner of the plastic bulge with a hair dryer first, then finish heating it further with a small lighter to make it pliable.
3. Wedge a small 2x4 between the heated fender and the tire to hold the plastic in place without pushing too hard into the material.
4. Move along the bottom edge of the bulge, repeating the hair dryer followed by the lighter heating sequence while slowly pushing inward with the 2x4.
5. Work higher up on the remaining portion of the bulge to push in as much of the largest plastic section as possible using the same heat and pressure method.
6. [Partial] Spray a small squirt bottle filled with ice water onto the area immediately after heating and applying pressure to help the plastic set quickly.

_Procedure reported by [t862]. Photos of this job are in the source: <https://www.xterranation.org/index.php?threads/how-to-the-melt-mod-33-tires-on-2nd-gen.2992/>_

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t1001] [Partial]</summary>

1. Wear safety glasses, earplugs, and gloves as per the power tool manufacturer's procedures.
2. Clean all areas to be welded until they are free of paint, grease, and rust.
3. Position the inner rings so their bottom surface is flush with the top lip on the wheel.
4. [Partial] Tack weld the assembly in four places to check its position.
5. [Partial] Weld around the entire circumference to seal everything up airtight.

</details>

- **Wheel Width (PRO-4X)**: DISPUTED, sources disagree: ~16" PRO-4X Wheel [t202]; ~16x8.5" MB TKO Wheel [t202]
- **Wheel Width (Titan)**: ~16x8.5" MB TKO Wheel [t202] ([Partial] [Unverified] single report)

## Tips & gotchas

- [Partial] Use a 2x4 instead of a hammer for better control and less risk of melting holes. [t862]
- Spray the area with ice water immediately after heating to speed up cooling and setting. [t862]
- Use power tools and proper PPE including safety glasses, earplugs, and gloves. [t1001]
- [Partial] Ensure inner rings are positioned to provide an excellent gap between metals for a good penetrating weld. [t1001]
- Consider upgrading to Load Range E if frequent off-roading over obstacles like tree stumps is expected. [t742]
- Be aware that heavier tires may slightly impact fuel economy compared to lighter options. [t742]
- [Partial] Note that these tires may feel like a 'paddle wheel' in deep water or monsoon conditions. [t742]
- They offer good performance in snow and mud while maintaining decent highway noise levels. [t742]
- [Partial] Be prepared for a slightly softer ride compared to C-load tires due to the heavier sidewall. [t742]
- [Partial] These tires offer a 50/50 balance between aggressive looks and all-weather handling. [t742]
- [Partial] They are generally heavier than stock sizes but provide excellent traction in mud, sand, and rock. [t742]
- These tires are well-mannered on the road despite being Load Range E. [t742]
- [Partial] They handle mud and snow exceptionally well. [t742]
- [Unverified value] Maintain tire pressure at 35 psi for around-town driving and 38 psi for long Interstate runs to minimize noise. [t431]
- [Unverified value] Air down the tires to 18 psi specifically for off-road use. [t431]
- Expect a bit of howling noise from the mud-terrain tread pattern. [t612]
- The wider tire and spacer combination will make the vehicle stance pop. [t612]
- [Partial] Expect the ride to feel stiffer and bouncier due to commercial load range. [t613]
- Run PSI about half of the max load for optimal handling balance. [t613]
- Use a Dremel with a grinding stone to clean up cut lines. [t623]
- Finish edges with 200 grit sandpaper for further cleaning. [t623]
- [Partial] Smash the pinch seam with a ball peen hammer (BFH) to bend it back. [t623]
- [Partial] Use a sponge and touch-up paint or bedliner on exposed metal before painting. [t623]
- Apply weather stripping along the new fender line for a clean look. [t623]
- [Partial] Use a rubber or vinyl material with a glue/resin track that presses into place (also known as Trim Guard). [t623]
- The front liner may need adjustment requiring more than the standard melt mod. [t748]
- Larger wheels provide less sidewall flex but weigh less than steel alternatives. [t748]
- Look for brands like Bora or Spidertrax that offer true hub/wheel-centric designs. [t214]
- Note that 2-inch spacers are less common in the most desirable hub/wheel-centric style. [t214]
- Note that Load Range E tires have a heavier sidewall compared to standard street options. [t209]
- Expect these tires to handle well in deep sand and rocky trails even at moderate pressures. [t209]
- [Unverified value] Verify cold pressures are within one pound of the specified 35 psi after cycling between hot and cool states. [t209]
- [Partial] Consider that a more compliant, less aggressive tire may require slightly different air pressure management than rugged all-terrains. [t209]
- Run these tires at lower pressures than standard specifications without fear of blowing a bead or sidewall issues. [t209]
- Accept that softer, stickier treads may offer better grip but potentially faster wear and more road noise. [t209]
- [Partial] Understand that the extra ply count provides sidewall protection, allowing you to air down further without worry. [t209]
- [Partial] Note that 10-ply tires may feel more compliant than standard street-oriented all-terrains. [t209]
- Ensure the original lugs are secured correctly on the adapters. [t743]
- Keep stock upper and lower control arms to maintain the original track width. [t743]
- Expect higher costs for new V8 half-shafts as they can be hard to find in salvage yards. [t743]
- A 33-inch tire usually fits fine, but a 35-inch requires about an extra inch of up-travel. [t743]
- Note that adding drop brackets lowers the differential by roughly 2 inches relative to the frame. [t743]
- [Partial] A 'melt mod' (fender trimming) is often needed for sizes 285 and up. [t745]
- Tires can be stretched to fit as large as a 305 width without major modification, though some fender trimming may still be required. [t745]
- [Partial] [Unverified value] Run tire pressure at 30-35 PSI for normal driving conditions. [t208]
- Note that P-series tires have softer sidewalls which improve handling compared to LTs. [t208]
- [Partial] Consider a 3-inch body lift if aiming for 35-inch tires instead. [t429]
- Note that 305/70/16 is an alternative size that fits well. [t429]
- [Partial] Aim for a tire diameter between 34 and 37 inches if off-pavement driving is the primary goal. [t439]
- [Partial] Expect to need at least a 35-inch tire on an 18-inch rim to air down effectively due to reduced sidewall. [t439]

## Common mistakes

- [Partial] Pushing directly into the plastic corner, which can melt through if not careful. [t862]
- [Partial] Neglecting rotation and re-balancing, which increases highway noise as tread wears. [t431]
- [Partial] Running factory specs too high without adjusting for commercial load range, causing a stiff ride. [t613]
- Ignoring that larger tires may stick out ~1/2 inch or ~10mm from the stock sidewall width. [t613]
- [Partial] Choosing tires that are too wide (like 305s) without accounting for the extra protrusion into wheel wells. [t745]
- [Partial] Expecting ice traction from all-terrain models like KM2s, which perform better on other surfaces. [t745]
- Choosing tires that are too small for the wheel size, resulting in less effective airing-down capabilities. [t439]
